keyVerseText: And the Midianites sold him into Egypt unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh's, and captain of the guard. officer: Heb. eunuch: but the word doth signify not only eunuchs, but also chamberlains, courtiers, and officers captain: or, chief marshal: Heb. chief of the slaughter men, or executioners
rootMeaning: The name פּוֹטִיפַר (Pôwṭîyphar) is of Egyptian derivation and literally means "belonging to the sun." This etymology points to a cultural and religious background tied to Egyptian sun worship, which contrasts with the worship of the one true God in Israel. The proper name thus carries a sense of foreign authority and power, rooted in an ancient Near Eastern context, which enriches its narrative role beyond a mere personal name.
usageInScripture: The word פּוֹטִיפַר appears only twice in Scripture, both times referring to the same individual—an Egyptian officer of Pharaoh who was Joseph's master after he was sold into slavery. The translations consistently identify him as "Potiphar" and highlight his role as an officer or chief executioner, emphasizing his high-ranking position in Pharaoh's court. This consistency underscores his importance as a figure of authority in the Genesis narrative, rather than a generic or symbolic character.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Potiphar's name as "belonging to the sun" and his role as a high-ranking Egyptian officer helps believers see the sovereignty of God working through foreign powers and circumstances to fulfill His purposes. Potiphar’s position as chief executioner and officer of Pharaoh situates Joseph’s trials within a divine providential framework, illustrating how God can use even pagan rulers and their servants to advance His redemptive plan. This reminds Christians that God’s providence extends over all earthly authorities, and that faithfulness in adversity can lead to God's ultimate blessing and deliverance.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 37:36 states that Joseph was sold "unto Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh's, and captain of the guard." The use of Potiphar’s name here identifies the specific Egyptian official who became Joseph’s master, emphasizing the reality of Joseph’s descent into slavery under a man of considerable power. The term "officer" (Hebrew eunuch) and "captain of the guard" (chief executioner) highlight Potiphar’s authoritative role, which sets the stage for the unfolding of God’s providential plan through Joseph’s life in Egypt.
